summary.text: A stratovolcano, also called a composite volcano, is a usually cone-shaped volcano built from many alternating layers of hardened lava and tephra.
Its lava is highly viscous, so it tends to cool and harden before spreading far, and the volcano has a steep profile with a summit crater.
Because its magma is too viscous for gas to escape easily, pressure from trapped gas builds up and eruptions are typically explosive.

items.prompt: As an ocean plate sinks into the mantle, minerals in it give off water. What does that water do to the hot mantle rock around it?

options.label: Cools it so it hardens into solid crust
Lowers its melting point so part of it melts
Turns to steam that blasts straight to the surface
Has no effect, as it boils off at once

items.explain: The released water lowers the mantle's melting point by 60 to 100 °C, letting it partly melt and form magma.

items.prompt: Why do stratovolcanoes such as Mount Pinatubo tend to erupt with explosive force rather than letting lava pour out gently?

options.label: Their magma is so runny that it races upward
Ocean water always floods their summit craters
Gas cannot escape their thick magma, so pressure builds
Their cones are too weak to hold any lava at all

items.explain: The magma is too viscous for gases to escape easily, so huge pressure builds until the vent breaks and the magma degasses explosively.

items.prompt: A road cut through an old volcano shows uneven, alternating bands of hardened lava and volcanic ash. Which kind of volcano is this most likely?

options.label: A stratovolcano
A shield volcano
A lava plateau
A cinder cone

items.explain: Stratovolcanoes are built of many alternating, often mixed and uneven layers of hardened lava and tephra, which is why they are also called composite volcanoes.

items.prompt: Fresh lava holds olivine crystals with no pyroxene rim, even though olivine quickly grows such a rim in silica-rich magma. What does this suggest?

options.label: The lava sat in its chamber for centuries
The olivine formed after the lava cooled
The magma had no silica in it at all
Fresh magma mixed in just before eruption

items.explain: A rim-free olivine crystal in silicic lava is only possible if the lava erupted immediately after mixing, so it is evidence of magma mixing right before eruptions.

items.prompt: A huge landslide strips away part of a volcano's flank. Which magma could this event set off?

options.label: Only magma in a very shallow chamber
Only magma in a very deep chamber
Magma at any depth, equally easily
No magma, as landslides never matter

items.explain: Sector collapse, where part of a volcano's flank fails in a massive landslide, can only trigger the eruption of a very shallow magma chamber.

items.prompt: Magma made in the mantle rises through the crust on its way to a stratovolcano. How does its makeup change on the way?

options.label: It loses its silica and becomes very runny
It takes in silica-rich crust and becomes intermediate
It stays exactly as it was in the mantle
It turns almost entirely into water and gas

items.explain: Rising magma incorporates silica-rich crustal rock, giving it a final intermediate composition.
